passage: Hafsa's cousin Nitin sent her a row of tiny yellow faces at 9 pm: 🙂🙂. Hafsa, eleven, stared at the screen from her bed in the Pune flat. Was he happy? Last week he used the same face when he lost at carrom and said "it's fine." She typed, "Are you ok?" Nitin replied with a crying face and then a heart, then, "Ha ha, I'm ok, just sleepy 😴." Hafsa laughed. "You use that smile for everything!" she wrote. Nitin sent a sticker of a dancing potato. Hafsa still wasn't sure which feeling the smiles meant, so she called him the next morning to hear his voice.

qa.q: What time did Nitin send the row of yellow faces?
qa.a: He sent them at 9 pm.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa ask "Are you ok?" after the smiling faces, and what might the faces really have meant?
qa.a: She remembered Nitin using the same face when he lost at carrom and said "it's fine", so she wondered if it hid a sad feeling. The faces might just have meant he was sleepy, as he said.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do when an emoji is unclear to her?
qa.a: She can ask, as she did, or call the person to hear their voice, rather than deciding what the emoji means on her own.

qa.q: How might Nitin see his smiling faces compared with how Hafsa read them?
qa.a: For Nitin the smile may be a simple all-purpose friendly sign. Hafsa read it as something with a possible hidden mood, so the same emoji meant different things to each.

grounding: A child uses smiling, crying and heart emoji and stickers for mood, and the same emoji is read differently by another person.

passage:
"Why did you send me a crying face, Zubin?" Ritu asked, holding up the tablet at dinner.
"Because I was sad. My tower fell."
"But it was the laughing-crying one. I thought you were laughing."
"It was crying and laughing. Both."
"Then how do I know?"
Zubin thought about it. "Maybe I'll write 'sad' next to it."
"Or send me the heart," said Ritu. "The heart means you love me."
"Bhaiya sent a heart to his teacher yesterday," said Zubin. "Does that mean he loves her?" Ritu burst out laughing. "Ask Papa!" 😄

qa.q: What happened to Zubin's tower?
qa.a: Zubin's tower fell.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he sent the crying face, and why did Ritu read it differently?
qa.a: Zubin felt sad and a bit amused that the tower fell, so Zubin meant both feelings. Ritu saw a laughing-crying face and thought Zubin was laughing.

qa.q: What could Zubin add so that Ritu understands the emoji better?
qa.a: Zubin could write a word like 'sad' next to the emoji, or say his feeling aloud, so the message does not depend on Ritu guessing.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel about needing to guess what the emoji means?
qa.a: Ritu feels confused and a little left out of Zubin's feelings, because Ritu cannot tell whether to comfort Zubin or laugh along.

grounding: A child sends emoji to convey mood, but the same emoji can be ambiguous to the receiver.

passage:
"Sahil, did you send Nani the voice note?" Keerthana asked.
"Yes, I sang the whole song."
"And you said 'Love you, Nani' at the end. She'll like that."
"But I made a mistake in the second line, so I sent it again."
"Nani won't mind. She likes hearing you."
"Will she show it to Aunty Lata? I sang in my funny voice."
Keerthana paused. "Ask her first. She can play it for herself, but you decide about others."
"Okay. Can I send a video of Bruno next?"
"Ask Nani if she wants it. And check that the dog isn't chewing your shoe." Sahil giggled. 🙂

qa.q: What did Sahil say at the end of the voice note?
qa.a: Sahil said, "Love you, Nani" at the end.

qa.q: Why was Sahil worried about the voice note being shared with Aunty Lata?
qa.a: Sahil sang in a funny voice and was afraid others might hear it, so wanted a say. Sahil seems to want to keep the fun for Nani only.

qa.q: What could Sahil do before sending a voice note or video to someone?
qa.a: Sahil could ask the person whether it is only for them, and think about whether it would feel okay if others heard it.

qa.q: How does Nani probably feel about hearing Sahil's voice?
qa.a: Nani probably feels warm and close to Sahil, because a voice carries warmth and tone in a way that a typed message doesn't.

grounding: A child sends voice notes and videos to family, showing warmth of voice and a reminder to think before sending because recordings can be forwarded.

passage: I'm Reena. Last winter I sent Yusuf a voice note from my grandmother's house. I was telling him about the snow and I said, "I miss you, you smell like a wet dog." I was joking. Yusuf sent back a heart and a laugh. But then my cousin heard it on his phone and told our whole class I had said Yusuf smells. I felt my stomach drop. Yusuf said it was okay, but I didn't record anything for a week. Now I think before I press send: would I be fine if other people hear it? Voice notes let people hear my smile, and I like that. 🙂

qa.q: What did Reena say in the voice note to Yusuf?
qa.a: Reena said, "I miss you, you smell like a wet dog," as a joke.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when Reena's cousin told the class about the voice note?
qa.a: Reena's stomach dropped, which suggests worry and embarrassment. Reena may also have felt guilty that the joke reached people it was not meant for.

qa.q: What could Reena do next time she wants to send a personal voice note?
qa.a: Reena could ask whether it would be fine if others heard it, and keep jokes for people who understand the tone.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have felt about the voice note and its spread?
qa.a: Yusuf answered warmly with a heart and a laugh and said it was okay, but he may also have felt awkward about being talked about at school.

grounding: A child values how voice notes carry warmth and tone, and learns that recordings can be forwarded so it is worth thinking before sending.

passage: Damini's bhangra class at the community hall had run for six weeks. Tanvir, the teacher, called the group to the front. "Again, from the top." Damini's shoulders lifted with the dhol beat and her feet stamped in the right place for the first time. She glanced around to see who'd noticed. Her face lit up, then shrank back when Tanvir said, "Good, but watch your arms." She frowned and repeated the step twice while the others waited. After class she was still practising by the door, sweat on her forehead, and grinning. "Tomorrow I'll get the arms right," she told her friend.

qa.q: How long had the bhangra class run?
qa.a: The bhangra class had run for six weeks.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she glanced around after getting the step right, and what does her frown suggest?
qa.a: She felt proud, shown by her lit-up face. The frown suggests some disappointment at the comment about her arms, though she still wanted to improve.

qa.q: What could Damini do to keep building her skill and confidence?
qa.a: She could keep practising the arm movements slowly, ask Tanvir to show them again, and enjoy the parts she now does well.

qa.q: What might Tanvir think when Damini stays on to practise by the door?
qa.a: Tanvir might see it as a sign that she cares and is willing to work, and may feel encouraged to keep teaching her.

grounding: A school-age child learns dance and finds that movement can carry pride and fun, with repetition building skill and confidence.

passage: Zainab watched her little sister Rehana from the sofa as she practised the harmonium in the corner. At first, Rehana pressed the keys with a stiff face, humming out of tune. After the tenth try, her shoulders dropped and her fingers slid more smoothly. She began to sway a little, eyes half-closed. When the tune reached the high note she smiled and glanced over. Zainab clapped. "It sounds like the rain song Nani used to sing!" Rehana went quiet, then said, "That's why I'm learning it." Zainab couldn't tell whether she was pleased or sad. Rehana played it again, and then again.

qa.q: Where did Rehana practise the harmonium?
qa.a: She practised in the corner while Zainab watched from the sofa.

qa.q: What did Rehana's quiet reply suggest she was thinking about Nani's song, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggests she was missing Nani and wanted to remember her through the song. Zainab could not tell if she was pleased or sad, so it might be both.

qa.q: What could Zainab do to support Rehana's practice?
qa.a: Zainab could listen and ask about the song, without pushing Rehana to explain, and let her play it as often as she likes.

qa.q: How does Zainab see Rehana's playing?
qa.a: Zainab notices Rehana's improvement and her swaying, and she is moved by the rain song, but she is unsure what Rehana feels.

grounding: A child learning an instrument finds sound can carry longing and pride, and repetition builds skill, seen by a sibling who cannot be certain of the feeling.

passage: My name is Tanuja. When I was ten, I played the mango seller in our school play. On the day, I walked on with my basket and said my first line, and someone in the front row laughed. I didn't expect it and forgot my second line for a second. I looked at Zeenat, our teacher, at the side of the stage. She mouthed the word and I said it louder than before. More people laughed and I noticed that the ones at the back were leaning forward. Later, when I said the sad line, they went completely silent. I couldn't tell if that was good or bad, but Zeenat said silence can mean they were listening.

qa.q: What role did Tanuja play in the school play?
qa.a: Tanuja played the mango seller.

qa.q: What did Tanuja think when the audience went silent during the sad line?
qa.a: Tanuja couldn't tell whether the silence was good or bad. Zeenat's remark suggests it could mean they were listening rather than bored.

qa.q: What could Tanuja try next time when she forgets a line?
qa.a: Tanuja could look at Zeenat at the side for the cue, take a breath, and keep going, as Tanuja did.

qa.q: How does Zeenat see the silence in the audience?
qa.a: Zeenat sees silence as a sign that people were paying attention, and helps Tanuja read it as engagement instead of a judgment.

grounding: A performing child notices laughter and silence, learns to adjust, and understands reactions as cues about engagement.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 6 play rehearsal. Ankita was the narrator in this afternoon's run-through for the parents' evening. In the first scene the audience of Class 3 children laughed at her funny voice, and she seemed to enjoy it and slowed down. In the second scene, some children began fidgeting and one yawned. I noticed Ankita's eyes flick to them and her voice speed up, then drop. I coached her after: "What did you see from the stage?" She said, "They got bored." I asked what she could try, and she suggested adding a pause and a louder line. We tried it. I will remind her that fidgeting tells us about the scene, not about her worth. Francis (stage manager) will time the next run. 🙂

qa.q: What role did Ankita have in the play?
qa.a: She was the narrator.

qa.q: What was Ankita likely thinking when she saw the children fidgeting and yawning, and what else might explain it?
qa.a: She likely thought they were bored, and her speeding up shows she was worried. The fidgeting might also come from the second scene being long or the children being tired.

qa.q: What could Ankita try when she notices restless children in the audience?
qa.a: She could add a pause, use a louder or livelier line, and adjust the pace, as she and the teacher tried after rehearsal.

qa.q: How might Francis help with the next run?
qa.a: As stage manager Francis will time the run, which gives Ankita information about the pace so she can adjust without taking the reaction as a verdict on herself.

grounding: A performing child notices laughter and fidgeting, adjusts, and is reminded that audience reactions are cues, not a verdict on worth.

passage: Sunday night. Recital tomorrow!! My hands are shaking a little and my mouth feels dry like chalk. Leela Ma'am said it is nerves and excitement mixed together, they feel the same in the body. She showed me to breathe in for four counts and out slowly, so I did it three times. It helped a bit. Then I played the whole Raag once for Amma, who sat there like a rock and smiled at the end. I still feel butterflies but they're smaller. I'll wear my blue kurta and look at Amma when I begin. If I mess up I will just go on. 🙂 — Chetan

qa.q: What colour kurta will Chetan wear to the recital?
qa.a: Chetan will wear a blue kurta.

qa.q: What did Chetan feel the night before the recital, and how could the shaking hands be read differently?
qa.a: Chetan felt nervous, with shaky hands and a dry mouth, and also excited. Leela Ma'am said the two feelings feel the same in the body.

qa.q: What could Chetan do on the recital day to help himself settle?
qa.a: Chetan could breathe slowly as practised, look at Amma at the start, and keep going after any mistake.

qa.q: How does playing for Amma help Chetan?
qa.a: Amma sits still and smiles at the end, giving Chetan a familiar friendly face and the confidence that the piece is fine.

grounding: A child before a recital shows shaking hands and a dry mouth, which reflect nervous excitement, and settles through slow breathing, rehearsal and a familiar face.

passage: At the temple fair in Anandpur, Kiran waited behind the curtain of the makeshift stage, holding her flute. Her hands trembled and her mouth was so dry that she took a sip from her steel glass. Her uncle Baljeet, who ran the sound system, crouched beside her. "Breathe in slowly," he said, "like smelling a flower. Out like blowing on hot chai." She did it three times. "Do you see Nani in the front row?" he asked. She peeked through the gap and Nani gave her a thumbs-up. Kiran's shoulders lowered a little. When her name was called she walked on, took a big breath, and began to play.

qa.q: Where did Kiran wait before her turn?
qa.a: She waited behind the curtain of the makeshift stage at the temple fair in Anandpur.

qa.q: Why did Kiran's hands tremble, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: She was probably nervous about performing, but the trembling can also be excitement. Her calmer shoulders after seeing Nani suggest fear was part of it.

qa.q: What could Kiran do if her nerves return before another performance?
qa.a: She could breathe slowly, look for a friendly face in the crowd, and rehearse the tune beforehand, as she and Baljeet did.

qa.q: How does Baljeet's help affect Kiran?
qa.a: Baljeet stays calm and gives simple breathing images, so Kiran does not feel alone. Seeing Nani helps her body settle.

grounding: A child before a recital shows shaking hands and a dry voice, and slow breathing and a friendly face help her settle.

passage: Pranav had been folding the paper boat since morning behind his father's tea stall at the bus stand. Twice it collapsed and twice he unfolded it, smoothing the creases with his thumb. He was making it for Vidya didi, who'd been ill and was going back to school tomorrow. He drew a small sun on the sail. When Vidya arrived, he held it out in both hands, avoiding her eyes. "It's lovely," she said. "I like the sun on the sail. And the sharp corners." Pranav's ears went red. "I did it three times," he said. Vidya smiled. "I can tell. I'll keep it on my desk."

qa.q: What did Pranav draw on the sail?
qa.a: He drew a small sun on the sail.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he handed over the boat, and what else might explain his red ears?
qa.a: He was probably proud and shy, since he avoided her eyes but told her he did it three times. The red ears might also be plain embarrassment at being watched.

qa.q: What kind of comment helps a child like Pranav most?
qa.a: A specific comment, like Vidya noticing the sun on the sail and the sharp corners, shows she looked closely and encourages him to keep making things.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel about receiving the boat?
qa.a: Vidya, who had been ill, probably feels cared for, since Pranav worked on it patiently for her and she says she will keep it on her desk.

grounding: A school-age child folds an origami boat with patience and care for a recipient, and a specific comment supports motivation.

passage: Beatriz had been building a cardboard model of the school bus for Lindiwe's birthday all week in the garage of their Lisbon house. She cut out windows, painted the wheels with yellow poster paint, and glued on paper passengers with names in tiny letters. When she brought it to the party, Lindiwe's uncle said, "Nice job!" and walked away. Beatriz's smile dimmed. Then Lindiwe crouched. "You put me at the front window! And the driver has my dad's moustache." Beatriz beamed. "I didn't know if you'd notice." Lindiwe set the bus on the shelf, next to her football trophy.

qa.q: What did Beatriz paint yellow on the model?
qa.a: She painted the wheels with yellow poster paint.

qa.q: What did Beatriz's dimmed smile suggest she felt after the uncle's comment, and why did she beam later?
qa.a: It suggests she felt a little disappointed that the comment was so general. She beamed when Lindiwe noticed the specific details she had worked hard on.

qa.q: What could Lindiwe's uncle say next time to encourage a child's effort?
qa.a: He could name something specific, like the painted wheels or the tiny names on the passengers, so the child knows the work was really seen.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel receiving the model?
qa.a: Lindiwe likely feels pleased and cared for because Beatriz put her at the front window and remembered her dad's moustache.

grounding: A child builds a model with pride, patience and care for the recipient, and specific comments support motivation better than general praise.

passage: In Class 5's art period at the city school, Mohit, the art teacher, held up a picture of a white bird with a leaf in its beak. "What do you think this means?" he asked. Divyansh raised his hand. "A pigeon that found food." A few children laughed. Mohit smiled. "Some people see a dove. In many places, a dove with a leaf means peace." Divyansh frowned. "But in my grandfather's village, a white bird means someone's coming." Mohit's eyebrows lifted. "That's a good thing to know. Symbols can mean different things, so we ask." Divyansh copied both meanings into his notebook.

qa.q: What was the bird in the picture carrying?
qa.a: The bird was carrying a leaf in its beak.

qa.q: What was Divyansh thinking when he frowned at the teacher's explanation, and what else could it show?
qa.a: He was likely comparing it with what he knew from his grandfather's village and realising his idea was also a real meaning. It could also show some embarrassment after the laughter.

qa.q: What could Mohit do to help children read symbols carefully?
qa.a: He could ask each child what a symbol means to them, list the different meanings, and remind them to check with others.

qa.q: How might the children who laughed feel after Mohit's response?
qa.a: They may feel a bit embarrassed, then curious, since Mohit showed that Divyansh's answer came from a real meaning in another place.

grounding: A child learns that a dove or other symbol stands for an idea and that symbols vary across cultures, so meaning must be checked.

passage: Yusuf's classmate Reena spent art period looking at a poster of a red cross. Yusuf noticed she stared at it a long time. "That means hospital," said a boy. "Or first aid," said someone else. Reena said, "In my grandmother's town, a red crescent is the same sign. My aunt works for it." The teacher hadn't said anything, but Reena's face looked serious. Yusuf wasn't sure what she felt; maybe she was thinking of her aunt. Then she drew a small heart on the corner of her own poster. "For helping," she said, and smiled a little. Yusuf copied the heart.

qa.q: What did Reena say her aunt works for?
qa.a: She said her aunt works for the red crescent.

qa.q: What might Reena have been feeling while staring at the poster, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: She may have felt proud or thoughtful about her aunt's work, since she linked the sign to her. She might also simply have been curious about the symbol.

qa.q: What could the class do when a symbol means different things to different people?
qa.a: They could ask each person what it means to them and note the different meanings, like Reena's red crescent, before deciding what a poster says.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see Reena's reaction to the poster?
qa.a: Yusuf can see she is serious and then a little smiling, but Yusuf isn't sure of her feelings and guesses she is thinking of her aunt.

grounding: A child learns that symbols such as a red cross or heart stand for ideas and vary across cultures, so their meaning must be checked.

passage: Hrithik, seven-year-old Tejas's older cousin, was doing homework when he noticed Tejas standing before the mirror for the third time that week, pushing his hair up with both hands. "He wants the same cut as Kabir in his class," Hrithik told his aunt. At the barber, Tejas pointed at a poster and said, "That one." His mother asked, "Are you sure? It's short on the sides." Tejas nodded hard and gripped the chair. When he came out, he kept touching the sides of his head and grinned at the mirror in the salon. He walked home a bit taller. Then he asked whether he could get the watch Kabir wears. His mother laughed. "One thing at a time."

qa.q: What did Tejas point at in the barber's shop?
qa.a: He pointed at a poster.

qa.q: Why did Tejas want the same haircut as Kabir, and what else might have been behind it?
qa.a: He seems to want to fit in with his classmates, shown by copying Kabir's style and later asking about Kabir's watch. He may also simply like the look.

qa.q: How could Tejas's mother balance his wishes with the family's budget?
qa.a: She could say yes to the haircut, talk about the watch and its cost, and let Tejas choose which small thing matters most to him.

qa.q: How does Hrithik see Tejas's mirror routine?
qa.a: Hrithik sees a cousin who is trying to look like a friend and finds it natural, so he explains it to his aunt rather than teasing.

grounding: A pre-teen wants a haircut or watch to match a classmate; the wish is normal and adults balance family values, budget and taste.

passage:
Day one. Payal, eleven, came home from school and asked Indu, her mother, for a smartwatch like her classmates. Indu said the family budget was tight. Payal went to her room and shut the door.

Day four. Indu suggested a simple digital watch from the market that they could pick together. Payal shrugged, but came along and tried a green one.

Day ten. Payal wore the watch to school. In the evening she told Indu, "Anaya has a smartwatch, but nobody cared. They liked my colour." She kept touching the strap all evening and was quiet, then asked if they could look for a cover to decorate it. Indu nodded. 🙂

qa.q: What kind of watch did Payal try in the market?
qa.a: Payal tried a green digital watch.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she shut her door on the first day, and how did it change by day ten?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and left out, and by day ten she seemed more settled because people liked her green watch. She may still have felt some wish for the smartwatch as she was quiet.

qa.q: What could Indu do to help Payal express her own taste?
qa.a: Indu could let Payal choose the strap or cover, listen to her worries about fitting in, and explain the budget without dismissing her wish.

qa.q: How might Indu feel about Payal's request?
qa.a: Indu probably feels torn between wanting to please Payal and staying within the budget, and is relieved when Payal accepts the market watch.

grounding: A pre-teen wants an accessory to fit in with classmates, and an adult balances budget and the child's taste over several days.

passage: Teacher's note: Arnab, Class 4. On the first day of the new term Arnab arrived in a uniform two sizes too big, with his older brother's worn black shoes. In the yard I watched him straighten his house badge and look at the other boys' shoes. When Rahul's new white sneakers were admired, Arnab put his hands behind him. At the badge ceremony, though, Gopika from his house squeezed in beside him, and Arnab stood tall and sang louder. I made a point of asking him to carry our house flag. He held it with both hands. I will keep an eye on how he feels about the shoes and talk to his parents if it keeps bothering him. 🙂

qa.q: What did Arnab straighten in the yard?
qa.a: He straightened his house badge.

qa.q: What did Arnab's hands behind his back suggest about how he felt about the sneakers, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggests he felt self-conscious about his old shoes. It could also just be a habit when standing in a group.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to support Arnab?
qa.a: The teacher can keep giving him roles that make him feel part of the house, watch how he feels about the shoes, and speak with his parents if the worry continues.

qa.q: How might Gopika see Arnab at the ceremony?
qa.a: Gopika, standing beside him, may see a fellow house member and simply include him. Gopika's closeness helps him feel he belongs.

grounding: A child sees a uniform and house badge signal membership, while still reading shoes as status cues.

passage: Monday night. New school, new uniform. Lalit's is the same as everyone's: grey trousers, white shirt, maroon tie. It felt strange but good, like being part of a team. At the gate the guard checked our ties, and I saw that Rohit's shoes were shiny and had a logo on the side. Mine are plain black and scratched. I tucked my feet under the desk in class. Then Sir said the house colours would be decided tomorrow and I got excited about being in a team. Maybe I'll be Red House. Amma polished my shoes tonight and said they looked new. I looked, and they did a bit. 🙂 — Chaitanya

qa.q: What colour tie is part of Chaitanya's uniform?
qa.a: The uniform includes a maroon tie.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya tuck both feet under the desk, and what else does the diary show Chaitanya felt about the uniform?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt self-conscious about the scratched plain shoes next to Rohit's shiny ones. The diary also shows Chaitanya felt good about the uniform, like being on a team.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya do if the shoe comparison keeps bothering Chaitanya?
qa.a: Chaitanya could talk to Amma or a teacher, and remember that the uniform makes everyone look alike apart from small things like shoes.

qa.q: How does Amma respond to Chaitanya's worry?
qa.a: Amma polishes Chaitanya's shoes and says they look new, a small, warm gesture that helps Chaitanya feel cared for.

grounding: A child notes that a uniform signals membership and reduces visible difference, yet still reads shoes as a status cue.

passage: The bell rang and Class 4 filed onto the school ground for morning assembly. Kavitha stood in the second row, palms flat against her skirt. When the anthem began, she sang the first line loudly and then lost the words. She looked to her friend Shalini, who mouthed the next line, and she caught up. A lamp was lit at the front by the head girl. Kavitha watched the flame and her shoulders relaxed. Afterwards she asked Shalini, "Why do we always light it?" Shalini said, "Ma'am says it's like starting the day with light." Kavitha nodded and thought. "I like the quiet part best." 🙂

qa.q: Where did Kavitha stand during assembly?
qa.a: Kavitha stood in the second row.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling as the lamp was lit, and what else might it be?
qa.a: Her shoulders relaxed, so she probably felt calm. She might also just have been relieved after losing the words to the anthem.

qa.q: What could an adult do to help a child find meaning in assembly rituals?
qa.a: They could explain what the lamp and anthem stand for, and let the child say what part feels special to them.

qa.q: How does Shalini help Kavitha during the anthem?
qa.a: Shalini mouths the next line so Kavitha can catch up, which shows a friend's quiet support during a shared ritual.

grounding: A child stands, sings the anthem and watches a lamp in morning assembly; the ritual gives shape to feeling and she asks what it means.

passage:
"Why do we have to stand so still for the anthem?" Yogesh asked in the car.
"To show respect," said Swati. "For the country, and for everyone standing with us."
"But I get itchy."
"Everyone does. It's only a minute. What do you notice when you do it?"
Yogesh thought. "My back gets straight. And I feel like we're all one thing."
"That's the point," Swati said. "What about the lamp?"
"I like it. It's warm and quiet."
He paused. "Can I stand beside Raj tomorrow? He always has the wrong words." Swati smiled. "I think he'd like that." 🙂

qa.q: Where did Yogesh ask his question about standing still?
qa.a: He asked it in the car.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he said his back gets straight and everyone feels like one thing, and what else did he mention feeling?
qa.a: He felt a sense of belonging and calm through the shared ritual. He also said he gets itchy standing still, so he feels a bit restless as well.

qa.q: What could Swati do to help Yogesh find meaning in the anthem?
qa.a: Swati could keep asking what Yogesh notices, as before, and let him describe the ritual in his own words before adding an explanation.

qa.q: How might Raj feel if Yogesh stands beside him?
qa.a: Raj may feel supported, because he always has the wrong words and would have a friend nearby.

grounding: A child explains what standing for the anthem and lighting a lamp feels like; ritual gives shape to feeling and he needs some explanation to find meaning.
